ny_f_the_guides_wall.blurb: A stretch of the Trapps, the main cliff of the Gunks, running from a huge orange right-facing corner at its left end to a prominent block just short of the next cluster of lines. The stone is the Gunks' quartz conglomerate: horizontal bands, jugs and roofs, with gear in the breaks. It is all trad, from very easy to solid 5.10, so beginners and experienced leaders alike find something here, mostly in one to three pitches. Spring and fall weekends bring crowds to the Trapps, while weekdays are far quieter. Summer foliage can hide the cliff from the carriage road below.
ny_f_the_guides_wall.parking_note: Two lots serve the Trapps: the West Trapps lot, reached by a connector trail from its far end up to the carriage road, or the lot past the Visitor Center, whose connector climbs a long run of stone steps to the same road. From the carriage road, short marked access trails lead to the base.

ny_d_strictly_the_ceiling.blurb: A section of the Trapps in the Gunks, bounded on the left by a sharp hanging arete and on the right by a large corner system where the next wall begins. It is almost entirely trad, from 5.3 up to the low 5.11s, with the bulk in the 5.7 to 5.10 range, and is best known for two moderate, classic lines that pull over big roofs. Radios help when partners go out of sight beneath the roofs. The rock is the Gunks' horizontally banded quartz conglomerate, with good gear in the breaks. Descent is by bolted rappel, and one rope is enough. Expect company on spring and fall weekends.
ny_d_strictly_the_ceiling.approach: From the lot past the Visitor Center, take the stone-stepped connector trail up to the carriage road, then turn onto the access trail at the Strictly junction. The first wall is directly above; the roofs are just around the arete to the right.

ny_sky_top.blurb: A long but fairly low cliff in the Gunks, tucked directly beneath the stone tower on the Sky Top summit near New Paltz. Routes run roughly 50 to 150 feet and are mainly trad, with some sport lines and top-ropes mixed in. Because the cliff sees little traffic, many lines are overgrown with lichen and carry no chalk, so expect to clean holds and move carefully. A footpath follows the base of the cliffs, winding through boulders and talus, and the summit tower sits a short scramble above. The climbing leans toward the middle grades, with a solid group of 5.8 to 5.10 lines and a handful of harder ones.

ny_upper_south_corner_cliffs.blurb: A cluster of small trad cliffs high on the southeast flank of Crane Mountain in the southern Adirondacks. The lines are mostly cracks, corners and overhangs from the easy 5s to 5.12, with the bulk between 5.7 and 5.10. Many of the walls are cleaned and well developed, though ledges between them stay brushy and some faces are dirty. The sun reaches the better walls well into the afternoon and they dry quickly. Be alert in winter and early spring, when ice builds in corners and under overhangs and can come down onto the cliffs below. Biting insects are heavy in May and June, and the hike to the cliffs takes a good while.
ny_upper_south_corner_cliffs.approach: Follow the unofficial East Path along the mountainside above the trailhead. A herd path branches off it near the Height-of-Land Wall and leads up to the Upper South Corner crags.

ny_east_face.blurb: The east side of Rat Rock, also called Umpire Rock, the best-known boulder in Central Park. It is a roughly 25-foot outcrop of Manhattan schist near the park's southwest corner, just west of the Heckscher ballfields. The east face holds a spread of problems from VB up through V6, with a few much harder lines at the top end. The schist is gritty and heights are modest. This is a popular urban spot, so expect other boulderers around, and it is an easy place to find partners for a session.

nc_cedar_rock_north.blurb: The north side of Cedar Rock, a steep granitic face in Pisgah National Forest near Brevard. This sector is mostly trad, with a few sport lines, a single aid line and a winter ice route in the mix. Most climbs fall between 5.8 and 5.11, with the heart of the sector around 5.9 and 5.10 and only a few easier or harder lines. The climbing is face and crack work on cedar-streaked stone in a forested setting, and lines tend to be steep and demand careful footwork. Summers are hot and humid, so mornings or late afternoons are the more comfortable choice; ticks and mosquitoes appear in warm months.

nc_cedar_rock_main_wall.blurb: The main cliff at Cedar Rock in Pisgah National Forest near Brevard, the wall you spot as you walk in from Butter Gap. It is mainly a trad venue with a couple of bolted sport lines, running from 5.5 to 5.12. The grade spread leans hard: a few easier lines, a solid group of 5.9 and 5.10, and the largest share at 5.11. Climbing is steep face and crack on granitic stone in a forest setting. Summers are hot and humid, so early or late in the day is more pleasant, and ticks and mosquitoes show up in warmer months.
nc_cedar_rock_main_wall.approach: Walk to the six-way intersection at Butter Gap and go straight across onto an unmarked old logging road. It leads up to the base of the main wall.

nc_north_end.blurb: A sector of Moore's Wall in Hanging Rock State Park, in the Sauratown Mountains of the Piedmont. The rock is quartzite, with sharp edges and holds that reward good footwork, and gear placements can be subtle. This end is mostly trad on shorter, steep routes aimed at intermediate to advanced leaders, with a couple of sport lines and a top-rope. Grades run from the 5.6 range up into the 5.13s, with most climbs between 5.10 and 5.12. A boulderfield lies downhill from the cliff. The wider Moore's Wall area is best in fall through early spring, when temperatures and friction are good, and it stays comparatively quiet.

_expect.name: The Dump aka Warpin and Dorphin (Routes)

nc_the_dump_aka_warpin_and_dorphin_route.blurb: A roadside sport crag in the High Country between Blowing Rock and Linville, with a short walk in. The rock is a metamorphic stone with edges, pockets and small crimps, and the cliff mixes steep walls and a roof with slabbier sections. Most routes are bolted sport climbs, with some trad lines and a top-rope. Climbs are short and reachy, and the harder ones are sustained puzzles. Grades cluster in the 5.10 to 5.12 range, with a good number at the top end and a few easier warm-ups. The cliff takes plenty of sun, which makes it a good winter choice, and the popular lines can get busy.
nc_the_dump_aka_warpin_and_dorphin_route.parking_note: The crag sits right beside US-221. Driving from the Blowing Rock side, watch for a wide dirt pull-off on the left a little beyond the Avery-Caldwell county line; the cliff is visible from it.
nc_the_dump_aka_warpin_and_dorphin_route.approach: A short, obvious trail climbs from the pull-off to the base of the wall.

_skipped.ny_table_rock: Only one page truly described the outdoor boulders; the others covered a campus hike or an indoor gym.
